books.section: Topic 8.11 The Civil Rights Movement Expands
Political Activism in the Latino Community

primary_sources: Indians of All Tribes, Proclamation to the Great White Father and All His People, November 1969 (paraphrased)
National Organization for Women, Statement of Purpose, 1966 (paraphrased)
Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, 438 U.S. 265 (1978) (paraphrased)
National Federation of State High School Associations, High School Athletics Participation Survey

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); the table is from the National Federation of State High School Associations; the photograph is public domain

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which movements for equality expanded the achievements of the civil rights movement from 1965 to 1980.

documents.title: Grapes and the boycott
documents.source: Account of the Delano grape strike and boycott, drawn from the grounding books and verified against National Park Service and EBSCO accounts.
documents.sourcing: The account is written from the farmworkers' side, so it stresses the tactics that won the contracts rather than the growers' view of the dispute.
documents.text: In September 1965, Filipino grape workers in Delano, California, went on strike for higher wages, and Cesar Chavez's National Farm Workers Association joined them. The strikers could not shut down the harvest alone, so the union asked shoppers across the country to stop buying California table grapes. In July 1970, growers signed contracts with the union, agreeing to higher wages and health and safety protections.

documents.title: Reclaiming Alcatraz
documents.source: Paraphrase of Indians of All Tribes, Proclamation to the Great White Father and All His People, November 1969.
documents.sourcing: The proclamation is addressed to the federal government, so it states the occupiers' claims in bold, public terms meant to be read by the whole country.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Proclamation to the Great White Father and All His People, November 1969. The occupiers reclaim Alcatraz Island in the name of all American Indians by right of discovery. They offer to buy the island for twenty-four dollars in glass beads and red cloth, following the white man's purchase of a similar island about 300 years ago. They say they will build an Indian school, cultural center, and museum there.

documents.title: Indian and proud
documents.source: Photograph: American Indian Movement member at the Wounded Knee occupation, 1973, public domain (Alliance Times-Herald photograph, via Wikimedia Commons).
documents.sourcing: The photograph shows an occupier from behind, with AIM and INDIAN AND PROUD on his jacket, so it presents the protest as the occupiers wanted to be seen: proud and armed.

documents.title: Women into the mainstream
documents.source: Paraphrase of the National Organization for Women, Statement of Purpose, 1966.
documents.sourcing: The statement is NOW's founding declaration, so it states the organization's aims as broadly as possible to gather support.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the National Organization for Women, Statement of Purpose, 1966. NOW declares its purpose is to bring women into full participation in the mainstream of American society, exercising all the privileges and responsibilities of citizenship in truly equal partnership with men.

documents.title: Girls take the field
documents.source: Table: Girls playing high school sports, National Federation of State High School Associations, High School Athletics Participation Survey.
documents.sourcing: The table comes from the federation that surveys high school sports, so it counts participation rather than arguing for Title IX.
documents.text: Girls playing high school sports. 1971-72: 294,015. 1977-78: more than 2,000,000. All high school athletes, boys and girls together: about 3.9 million in 1971-72; about 6.4 million in 1977-78. Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 banned sex discrimination in any education program receiving federal money.

documents.title: The limits of remedy
documents.source: Paraphrase of Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, 438 U.S. 265 (1978).
documents.sourcing: The decision is a Supreme Court ruling, so its words show what the law allowed and forbade, not what either side in the case hoped for.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, decided June 28, 1978. The University of California at Davis had set aside 16 of its 100 medical school places each year for minority applicants. The Court ruled that the fixed quota was unconstitutional, but that race could be one factor among others in admissions decisions.

documents.title: Fighting back at Stonewall
documents.source: Account of the Stonewall Inn raid and the Gay Liberation Front, drawn from the grounding books and verified against Washington University Becker Library accounts.
documents.sourcing: The account is written after Stonewall became a symbol, so it stresses the turning point rather than the everyday harassment that came before it.
documents.text: In the early morning of June 28, 1969, New York City police raided the Stonewall Inn, a bar in Greenwich Village that served gay men and lesbians. Raids on such bars were common, but this time the patrons fought back, and crowds gathered outside for several nights. In the weeks that followed, activists formed the Gay Liberation Front, which protested press coverage of gay people and challenged the classification of homosexuality as a mental disorder.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which movements for equality expanded the achievements of the civil rights movement, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Black civil rights movement of the 1960s, the growth of federal power, or the social upheavals of the late 1960s.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (first point): earns the point for describing specific examples from at least three documents that support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without using their content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (outside evidence): earns the point for describing at least one specific piece of evidence beyond the documents that supports the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating a document's content as outside evidence does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience of at least one document shapes what it says.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how that shapes the document does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for showing a complex understanding, such as explaining both expansion and limits, or qualifying the argument with evidence that cuts the other way.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument with no qualification or counter-evidence does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Movements for equality greatly expanded the civil rights movement's achievements by carrying its tactics and ideas to new groups, but they also met limits, in the courts and in public resistance, that kept the expansion unfinished.
Grouping: Documents 1-3 show the expansion to farmworkers and Native Americans (grape boycott, Alcatraz, Wounded Knee); Documents 4-5 show the expansion to women (NOW, Title IX table); Documents 6-7 show expansion and its limits (Bakke, Stonewall).
Outside evidence: Background: The Equal Rights Amendment passed Congress in 1972 but fell three states short of ratification by 1982; the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act of 1975 let tribes run their own programs; the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from its list of mental disorders in 1973.
Complexity: The same period that opened schools and jobs to new groups also produced Bakke's limit on quotas, so the expansion was real and contested at once. Background: Resistance to busing sometimes turned violent, as in Boston in 1974.
